VANCOUVER,
B.C.

On December 15, 1992, I delivered
brief written reasons transferring sole custody of Samantha from her mother to
her father.  I indicated that I would provide fuller reasons for judgment
shortly thereafter.  Those reasons follow.

BACKGROUND:

Both parties sought sole custody
of  their daughter Samantha who was born on November 13, 1987.  Mr. Gurvin, the
plaintiff, and Ms. Tingren, the defendant, were never married and they never
co-habited.   Until December 15, 1992, Samantha  had always lived with her
mother and, since May 1990, with both her mother and Mr. Gidley, her mother's
common-law husband.  Her half-brother Dougie was born on February 11, 1991.
Between February 24, 1991 and December 15, 1992, all visits between Samantha
and her father were supervised.

The major issues in this case
arose from the defendant's allegations that the plaintiff had sexually abused
his daughter and the plaintiff's concern that Ms. Tingren had repeatedly and
continuously attempted to destroy the relationship between him and his
daughter.  A further protection concern arose from disclosures made by Samantha
that Mr. Gidley had beaten Ms. Tingren in Samantha's presence, and that he had
beaten Samantha and locked her in her room.

The parties met in 1983 and
began a relationship which ended when Ms. Tingren discovered that Mr. Gurvin
was living with another woman.  They began dating again in August 1986 and very
soon thereafter, Ms. Tingren became pregnant.  They dated until March 1987.  It
is common ground that Mr. Gurvin urged her to obtain an abortion.  Although the
plaintiff testified that he assured Ms. Tingren that he would support her
financially and emotionally if she chose to bear the child, I prefer her
evidence that he was very upset about her pregnancy and persisted in urging her
to have an abortion.  He admitted that he was not supportive during her
pregnancy in an interview with Dr. Elterman, a clinical and consulting
psychologist who completed a psychological assessment of the parties and
Samantha.

Shortly before Samantha's birth,
Ms. Tingren became very ill and the baby was delivered prematurely by caesarean
operation.  To her surprise, Mr. Gurvin, who had been called by a friend, Ms.
Cividino, arrived at the hospital and attended Samantha's birth.  He took
Samantha and Ms. Tingren home and, for the next two years, visited them
frequently, sometimes staying overnight.  He helped with childcare and cooking
and described his involvement as co-parenting Samantha.  Ms. Tingren described
that phase, during which Mr. Gurvin had his own key, as his "coming and
going whenever he pleased."  Her closest friends, who visited her
regularly during that period, testified that Mr. Gurvin was rarely present.  I
find that his participation in the lives of Samantha and her mother was more
frequent than described by Ms. Tingren's friends but that it was dictated
solely by his convenience.

I accept Ms. Tingren's evidence
that Mr. Gurvin did not tell his mother about the baby until her birth and that
after he did so, he obeyed her wishes that Samantha's existence be kept secret
from the rest of the family.  Ms. Rubin, who worked at the family business,
Gurvin's Jewellers, between September 1987 and April 1989 understood that Mrs.
Gurvin was very upset because Ms. Tingren was not Jewish and because she and
Mr. Gurvin were not married.  Ms. Rubin was surprised when she learned that the
plaintiff had a baby approximately 8 months old.

Ms. Rubin also testified that Mr.
Gurvin had engaged in several casual amorous relationships during the period
that she worked at Gurvin's Jewellers.

In February 1990, Ms. Tingren
became aware that Mr. Gurvin was seeing other women and broke off their
relationship.  I conclude that, up to that time, Mr. Gurvin had been a most
unsatisfactory companion and parent.  However, in the two years following
Samantha's birth, Mr. Gurvin had formed an attachment to his daughter which he
became increasingly reluctant to lose.  In the absence of a relationship with
Ms. Tingren, he had to rely upon his parental right of access in order to
continue seeing Samantha.  Notwithstanding its tenuous beginnings, that
attachment was to grow into a warm, loving father-daughter relationship.

Ms. Tingren testified that in
March 1990, the plaintiff decided to take a more active role in Samantha's
life.  She attributed the timing of his sudden interest in Samantha to her new
relationship with Mr. Gidley.  I attribute Mr. Gurvin's "sudden
interest"  to his recognition that unless he exercised his parental rights
diligently and responsibly, he would lose them.

After hearing 19 days of evidence,
I concluded that Ms. Tingren's anger and frustration with Mr. Gurvin's refusal
to be a loving and supportive helpmate in Samantha's  early years developed
into a rancorous resentment toward his  subsequent determination to be a part
of Samantha's life.

ACCESS BEFORE SUPERVISION:

The plaintiff testified that he
exercised access without incident until March 1990.  At that time, he offered
to take Samantha for four days to assist Ms. Tingren who was experiencing
stress as a result of returning to employment and caring for the baby.

Ms. Tingren expressed concern
about two events which occurred during that overnight access:  Mr. Gurvin
bathed with Samantha who was then 2 years old, and he let her sleep with him in
his queen-size bed because he worried that she might be afraid if she woke in
the night in a strange place.   He saw nothing wrong with those activities.
Samantha slept soundly through the night and he had showered with her
previously, at times when Ms. Tingren was in the bathroom and when she was
not.  I accept his evidence that he did not bathe or shower with Samantha after
the defendant expressed her concerns.

Ms. Tingren testified that after
the overnight visits in March, Samantha became very withdrawn and exhibited
strange behaviour such as sitting in her doll's buggy and sucking her thumb.
She developed night terrors and wet her bed and her pants in the day although
she had been fully toilet trained.  Ms. Tingren felt that the transition to
overnight access had been too abrupt as Samantha had spent little time with her
father up to that point.

After March 1990, Ms. Tingren
began systematically restricting or denying the plaintiff's access.  No further
overnight access was permitted.  Mr. Gurvin attributed the restrictions on his
access  to Mr. Gidley's influence.

Mr. Gidley and Ms. Tingren had
begun dating in February 1990 and he moved into her house in May of that year.
On one occasion early in that relationship, Mr. Gidley told the plaintiff:
"You have to earn the right to see your daughter."  Communication
between the two men became severely strained to the extent that Mr. Gidley told
Mr. Gurvin not to set foot on his property.  The friction appears to have been
exacerbated by Samantha calling the plaintiff "Daddy Michael" and Mr.
Gidley "Daddy Jim."

In the spring of 1989, Ms.
Tingren  had made plans to move to Ontario with Samantha to be close to her
family.  The plaintiff had not objected to that move but Ms. Tingren decided to
stay in British Columbia.  In July 1990, Mr. Gurvin became concerned that she
would move east with Samantha.  Seeking to exercise a larger and more
predictable role in Samantha's life, he commenced an action for joint custody
and joint guardianship.  In that action, he sought and obtained a restraining
order preventing Ms. Tingren from taking the child out of the jurisdiction.

Ms. Tingren commenced a separate
action seeking sole custody the day after the plaintiff issued the writ in the
first action.  Mr. Gurvin then learned, for the first time, through the
affidavits filed by Ms. Tingren, of her allegations of the plaintiff's
inappropriate conduct, her concern that he drank and drove, and her complaints
about his lack of involvement in Samantha's life.

Master Patterson awarded the
defendant interim custody on July 16, 1990 and he made further orders granting
specified unsupervised access to the plaintiff, preventing him from bathing or
showering with Samantha, ordering him to pay the monthly sum of $400.00 child
support, and directing that a Section 15 Report be prepared pursuant to the
Family
Relations Act
.

Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley
testified that after that time, but before supervised access was ordered, Mr.
Gurvin brought pictures of Samantha in the bath tub, flaunting the court
order.  As that alleged incident was not put to Mr. Gurvin to agree or deny or
explain, and that concern was not expressed to Dr. Elterman, I do not place any
weight on that evidence.

Ms. Watty prepared a Section 15
Report on August 17, 1990.  She observed that the defendant  appeared "to
harbour a fair amount of animosity toward Mr. Gurvin."  Ms. Tingren told
her that she did not believe that Mr. Gurvin really wanted to see Samantha but
had some ulterior motive unknown to her.  Ms. Watty recommended that a
psychological evaluation of Samantha and her parents be prepared.  In the
circumstances of the parties' relationship with Samantha and with each other,
she did not consider joint custody or guardianship appropriate.

Ms. Tingren testified that in
December 1990, when Samantha was barely three years old, she began to engage in
excessive masturbation and became preoccupied with her sexual organs.  She said
that after the visits with her father, Samantha had a very red vagina and was
constantly masturbating.  On one occasion, when she offered to put vaseline on
Samantha's vagina, Samantha said "oh, no, Daddy Michael will" and
indicated that he had done it before.  Ms. Tingren took Samantha to Dr.
Mitchell, a family practitioner, on January 19, 1991 expressing concern that
she had been sexually abused.  His examination of her stomach, vaginal area and
anal area was normal.  Both Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley testified that after the
next visit on January 27, 1991, Samantha complained of a sore bum and was
otherwise quiet and withdrawn.  Ms. Tingren observed a red ring around her
anus.  Ms. Tingren testified that Samantha woke up at 1:00 in the morning
screaming "play doctor" with Daddy Michael."  Mr. Gidley
testified that she said "Daddy Michael hurt my bum."

On the following day, she took
Samantha to Dr. Mitchell.  He testified at trial that he observed a condition
known as erythema, a red ring, 5 cm. in diameter around her anus.  The redness
was not raised.  The anus and surrounding tissues were normal and there was no
pain.  He enumerated a number of causes which he was unable to rank in order of
probability:  physical stimulation by the child or by another person; chemical
contact; persisting irritation resulting from the area not being cleaned after
urination or bowel movement; and sand in a bathing suit.

Dr. Mitchell wrote a letter which
was appended to the defendant's affidavit in support of an application to halt
access.  In it, he stated:  "This abnormality may have resulted from
sexual abuse.  The child states her father touched her bottom."  At trial,
he testified that he did not recall Samantha making that statement.  He had
simply reiterated what he had been told by Ms. Tingren.

Ms. Krause babysat Samantha for a
couple of months  during the period of time that Mr. Gurvin exercised overnight
access in March 1990.  She  described some incidents involving bizarre and
abnormal behaviour by Samantha which I do not propose to relate.  I found her
evidence, which was delivered in an extremely melodramatic and artificial
manner, to be fantastical and unworthy of credit.  An affidavit describing some
of those incidents was sworn and filed in March 1992 in opposition to the
plaintiff's application for unsupervised access.  It is curious that such an
affidavit was not prepared to support Ms. Tingren's concerns of sexual abuse in
January 1991.

SUPERVISED ACCESS
:

Following the defendant's
application, Master Kirkpatrick suspended access on January 30, 1991.  On
February 20, 1991, Master Doolan ordered that all access visits be supervised
by the Greater Vancouver Mediation and Supervisory Services.   That agency,
which Ms. Jane Grafton has operated for the past seven years, supervises access
visits pursuant to a court order or by agreement of the parties.  Ms. Grafton
supervised the plaintiff's visits with Samantha until May 1991 and Ms. Ann
Scott supervised all or most of the visits from October 1991 until December 15,
1992.  Neither supervisor observed any improprieties on the visits.  Their
policy  in all cases where sexual abuse is alleged is to stay with the child,
to ensure that the child is not left alone with the access parent, and to
prevent whispering and any discussion about the custodial parent.

Ms. Grafton assured Ms. Tingren
that Samantha would never be left alone with the plaintiff and that both
counsel would receive reports every two weeks.  Ms. Grafton supplied reports of
the visits to counsel for both parties until July 1992, at which time she made
a general policy decision not to provide reports except in special
circumstances.  I accept her evidence that she told Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley
of her decision not to supply further reports despite their denial of that
fact.  However, in the circumstances of this case, that decision proved
unfortunate.  Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley became increasingly dissatisfied with
the supervision and it was inevitable that their discontent, albeit largely
unjustified,  would increase as a result of a sudden absence of any reports.
In retrospect, it would have been better if Ms. Grafton had implemented her new
non-reporting policy with new clients rather than clients who were accustomed
to receiving the reports.

The supervisors' reports raised a
number of very serious concerns.  Commencing in late October l991, Samantha
began making disclosures to Ms. Scott.  The following passages are taken from
those reports:

Access
visit:  October 29/91:
Samantha said "I'm just a little girl and Cheryl shouldn't yell
at me so much.  Michael never yells at me."

Access
visit:  November 19/91:
Samantha said:  "But Daddy Jim hits me and it hurts me and I
cry.  Then he locks me in my room."

"My
mummy yells at me all the time and Jim and Mummy say I'm always bad."

Access
visit:  November 21/9l:
Ms. Scott went to pick up Samantha for a visit.  She was playing
with the baby Dougie and Samantha joined in.  "Jim [Gidley] yelled at
Samantha and told her to leave Dougie alone.  Samantha lowered to the floor in
a fetal position covering her head."  A second time Mr. Gidley yelled at
her, raising his hand and saying, 'Sam, you'll be sorry if you don't listen.
Now don't do that again.'  Samantha again dropped to the floor in a fetal
position covering her head."  In her direct evidence, Ms. Scott said that
Samantha cowered like a dog.  In the car she said "I'm always bad and
Mummy and Jim always yell at me."

For reasons which are not clear
to me, the reports of those visits were not supplied to the parties until
February 1992.

Ms. Tingren's explanation for the
scene that Ms. Scott witnessed was that  Samantha is a very dramatic child who
over-reacts and stages a tantrum or becomes hysterical if anyone lays a hand on
her.  She said that Samantha became hyperactive before her visits with the
plaintiff and on that day, she had been pulling on Dougie despite Mr. Gidley's
repeated admonitions to stop.  When he put his hand up, she became very
dramatic and fell to the floor.  Mr. Gidley gave a similar explanation.  He
said that he had raised his voice but did not yell.  He had raised his hand but
did not strike her.  He did not know if she had fallen to the ground in
anticipation that he might strike her.

Ms. Scott, who has extensive
experience with children both professionally and as a mother,  was extremely
concerned to hear Samantha's disclosures that she had been beaten and locked in
her room.  She believed that Samantha was neither exaggerating nor telling a
story.  At the time, she did not tell either  parent but instead she told Ms.
Grafton and Dr. Elterman.  In her view, those disclosures were confirmed by the
incident she observed on November 21, 1991.

Ms. Scott had frequently returned
Samantha to Mr. Gidley when Ms. Tingren was not there.  She was not comfortable
with Mr. Gidley and described Ms. Tingren as less friendly and very abrupt when
he was present.

Ms. Scott made the following
report after the access visit of February 18/92:

Samantha
said "Daddy, you hurt me in my vagina, didn't you?"  Mr. Gurvin said
"No. I didn't.  I never touched you there, ever."  When he asked why
she thought that, she said "Because Cheryl said you hurt my vagina."
"Mummy tells me at breakfast in the morning when I'm eating.  Mummy says
that's why you're not allowed in our house. . . .But I don't remember. . . No,
Michael never hurts me."

Later
that day, "Daddy, it's ok if you put vaseline on my vagina."

On
the way home:  "Jim's quit hitting me. . . Jim's quit being mean to me and
hurting me. . . Cheryl says he's going to be nice and not spank me any
more."

Those statements clearly reflect
Ms. Tingren's attempts to coach Samantha to make disclosures of sexual abuse by
her father. They also reflect a concern by Ms. Tingren that Samantha's
disclosures of conflict in the Gidley-Tingren household were being taken
seriously.

A number of reports which were
delivered under cover of a letter dated April 6, 1992 contained the following
disclosures:

Access
visit:  March 17/92:

Samantha said "Jim doesn't like you Daddy, but I do.  . . Jim is bad to me
but you never hurt me."

Access
visit: March 24/92:

On the drive home, Samantha said "It would be ok if I slept over at Daddy
Michael's house because he is always good to me and he never hurts me; just Jim
hurts me.  Jim spanks me and hits me and locks me in my bedroom when I'm bad.
Jim thinks I'm always bad."

Access
visit:  March 26/92:
When
Samantha took off her clothes to try on her bathing suit, Ms. Scott noticed
that her vaginal area was very red and Samantha said "I have a cute
vagina, don't I?  Mummy says so.  Jim likes my vagina too.  He likes to look at
it."  She asked Nicole [Mr. Gurvin's girlfriend] if she thought she had a
cute vagina and Nicole said "I guess so."

The reports sent out on May 28,
1992 contain the following references:

Access visit: May 19/92:
"Daddy, Jim is always hitting
Mummy.  Can you stop Jim from hitting my Mummy?"

Access
visit: May 21/92:

"Sometimes when Jim hits Mummy she gets mad and sad too, then she says
'don't hit me' and she hits him back.  Then they fight a whole bunch and it
makes me sad too and I cry."

Ms.  Tingren and Mr. Gidley did
not believe that Samantha made those disclosures and they both vehemently
denied that he had ever hit her.

On February 25, 1992, shortly
after the  reports for October 1991 through January 1992 setting out Samantha's
disclosures were sent in a bundle on February 11, 1992, Mr. Gidley told Ms. Scott
there would be no visit that day; he gave her a letter addressed  to Ms.
Grafton.   In it, he said that visits were suspended until the agency provided
reports of all visits.  Two days later, Ms. Tingren again refused to let
Samantha visit her father because she did not have the reports.

A report dated March 17, 1992
described Samantha's  complaints that her vagina and bottom were sore on the
visit of February 20, 1992.  She told Ms. Scott to look and see how red those
parts of her body were and later asked Mr. Gurvin to put vaseline on them.  Mr.
Gurvin told her to tell her mum.  Ms. Scott phoned Dr. Elterman the next
morning to report this and asked for instructions from counsel.

On March 31, 1992, Ms. Tingren
and Mr. Gidley purported to fire Ms. Grafton's agency and sought to institute a
supervisor of their choice, Mr. Foyle.  He is a retired police officer who
presently operates his own business as a private detective and security
consultant.  At the time of trial, he had supervised one young boy.

In a subsequent affidavit, Ms.
Tingren deposed that the unilateral change in supervision was made in the best
interests of her daughter:  "In the face of most unusual if not deceitful
behaviour on the part of the supervisors their credibility was strained to the
limit."

At trial, Ms. Tingren and Mr.
Gidley expressed extreme displeasure with the quality of the supervision.
They voiced a number of specific complaints:

(a)
On one visit, Mr. Gurvin had taken Samantha and another child on a very brief
foray through a "haunted house" in a shopping mall while the
supervisor remained outside.  Ms. Grafton agreed that the supervisor should
have accompanied Mr. Gurvin and Samantha through the haunted house because her
responsibility was to oversee 100% of the interaction between parent and child
on such visits.  However, I am satisfied that nothing untoward could possibly
have happened in the circumstances of that occasion.

(b) On another occasion, when Ms.
Tingren was detained,

the
supervisor returned Samantha by leaving her with a neighbour whom she did not
know well.  The supervisor apparently did so because she would otherwise have
been late for another access visit.

(c)
During one visit, Ms. Scott permitted the plaintiff to hold Samantha on his lap
in a darkened movie theatre  although she sat beside them in the next seat.

(d)
During a number of access visits, Ms. Scott took Samantha to be interviewed by
Dr. Elterman for an update of his report without Ms. Tingren's knowledge.

(e)
After one visit, Ms. Scott told Ms. Tingren that Samantha had fallen and hurt
herself even though she, Ms. Scott, had been behind her.  She said that
Samantha responded "No, you weren't" and later told her that at the
time of her fall, Ms. Scott and the plaintiff were in his bedroom folding
towels.

Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley
testified that they became increasingly disenchanted with the supervisory
agency. They  decided that Ms. Scott had moved from a neutral to a biased
position which favoured Mr. Gurvin.  Mr. Gidley testified that "it felt
like a war with Jane Grafton, Ann Scott and Michael Gurvin."

When Ms. Scott arrived to pick up
Samantha on March 31, 1992,  she was told that the agency's services had been
terminated and that Mr. Foyle would supervise future visits.  Ms. Tingren and
Mr. Gidley used the fact that Mr. Gurvin proposed to take Samantha on a short
boat trip as the specific reason for changing supervisors.  Mr. Gidley
testified that he had heard Master Tokarek say that they could change
supervisors.  In fact, Master Tokarek stated in his reasons of March 10, 1992
that the defendant could bring a court application for a change in
supervision.  He added:

But
until you apply and obtain such an order this supervisor can continue the supervision
and access will not be interfered with because you are considering or bringing
on an application.

The plaintiff considered Mr.
Foyle unacceptable as a supervisor because he knew nothing about him and he was
concerned that a change in supervision would create one more change in
Samantha's troubled life.  The defendant denied access on March 31, April 7,
and April 16, 1992.    Ms. Andres-Auger, in her letter of April 2, 1992, took
the position that her client was free to change the supervision unilaterally
and that it was Mr. Gurvin who had failed to exercise access:

Since
my client had no problem in respect of Mr. Gurvin's continuing supervised
access, it must be your client that perceives a problem of sufficient gravity
to warrant his refusal to exercise access.  My client has not been instrumental
in any discouragement your client may be experiencing.

She noted that Mr. Foyle was
still available and concluded:

If
we do not hear from you by Monday, April 6, 1992 a clear message that your
client wishes to resume access visits, we shall presume that he is too
discouraged to continue.

There is no question that the
defendant was strenuously and continuously seeking to "discourage"
Mr. Gurvin from exercising the access to which he was entitled.  Further court
proceedings on April 6, 1992 resulted in the resumption of access.  As a result
of Ms. Tingren's denial of access during this period, Mr. Justice Warren found her
to be in contempt of the Orders of Masters Doolan and Tokarek.

In hindsight, as I have noted,
there are incidents which should have been avoided (e.g., the incursion into
the haunted house and the delivery of Samantha to a neighbour in Ms. Tingren's
absence).  Further, the reports should have been supplied in a more timely
fashion and it would have been preferable if the  reports had continued.
However, on the whole, there is very little basis for the defendant's
dissatisfaction with the supervision.   I reject Ms. Andres-Auger's submission
that Ms. Scott lost her neutrality and impartiality as a supervisor and became
partisan and biased.  After reviewing all of the reports and hearing the
evidence of Ms. Grafton and Ms. Scott, I conclude that the supervisors
conducted themselves responsibly, impartially and professionally.  I consider
also that the reports accurately reflect the incidents which are related
therein.

THE DEFENDANT AS A PARENT:

Ms. Tingren is 38 years old.  She
is the second of four children in her family.  She was raised in Ontario where
most of her family continues to reside.  She has worked extensively in the car
business and she was the business manager at a Nissan dealership at the time
Samantha was born.  Although she returned to work in early 1990, she
subsequently considered it necessary to stay at home in light of the alarming
changes she observed in Samantha's behaviour.

Mr. Gidley and Ms. Tingren first
met when she was pregnant in 1987.  He hired her as a part-time business
manager in January 1990 and shortly thereafter they began to date.  They
commenced living together in May 1990 and their son Dougie was born on February
11, 1991.  Although they intend to marry, they testified that they have been
unable to make plans while this litigation is ongoing.

Ms. Tingren described Samantha as
a happy, sociable child who was not aggressive before she commenced her visits
with the plaintiff.  After that time, she depicted Samantha as increasingly
aggressive and mean to other children, particularly to her brother Dougie whom
she had recently thrown down the stairs.  She destroyed her toys, and was so
cruel to their pet dog that they gave it away.  Bedtimes were particularly
difficult.  After January 1991, she began talking about jail and trying to tie
up everyone who came into the house.  She apparently behaved strangely after
visits.

Samantha's behaviour problems
were confirmed by witnesses who are frequent visitors to the Tingren-Gidley
household.  They dated those problems variously from the fall of 1989, 1990 and
sometime within the last year.  They described incidents of Samantha babbling
or talking baby talk, acting destructively or meanly to  other children.  They
considered her belligerent, difficult and constantly seeking attention.  They
all characterized the defendant as a patient, loving and tolerant mother.  Ms.
Tingren had told them of her belief that the plaintiff sexually assaulted
Samantha and they associated the changes they have observed in Samantha's behaviour
to that cause.  Regrettably, it appeared from the evidence of at least one of
the witnesses, that Ms. Tingren may have discussed the sexual abuse allegations
in Samantha's presence.  Most of her friends agreed that Ms. Tingren has been
frustrated and angry with the plaintiff since January 1991.

Ms. Tingren said that Samantha
was unresponsive to discipline.  Samantha pushed her to her limit and she began
spanking Samantha when she was 2 1/2 as "a last resort."  When
Samantha hurt her brother she received a spanking either with a wooden spoon or
spatula on her hand or a hand on the bottom.  She said that Mr. Gidley had also
spanked Samantha on occasion, for hurting Dougie or the dog or refusing to stay
away from the stove, but that he had never struck her in anger.

When Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley
moved into their present home, all the bedroom doors had hooks and eyes on the
outside but she denied that she locked Samantha in her room.  She described
sending Samantha to her room to sit quietly when she misbehaved and her
subsequent frustration when the child refused to stay in her room.  At her
examination for discovery, the defendant had testified that she had put the
lock on the door because no other discipline methods had worked.  She testified
at that time that "we only had to use it a few times."   Although she
denied those statements at trial, I find that the defendant and Mr. Gidley have
locked the child in her room.

Ms. Tingren testified that before
the trial she was prepared to continue access but, during the course of the
trial, she had decided that access was not in Samantha's best interests because
it was detrimental and increasingly confusing to her.  She said that Samantha's
behaviour had improved markedly when she had taken her to Ontario for two weeks
in September 1991 to visit her family because her grandmother was ill.  (That
visit, which was undertaken without leave of the court or the consent of the
plaintiff, was in breach of the restraining order of this Court made in July
1990).

Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley both
expressed the belief that Samantha's behaviour would normalize if access were
cut off.

Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley
believe that Mr. Gurvin gives Samantha anything she wants, including toys,
excessive physical affection and junkfood which made her unruly and demanding
at home.  Ms. Tingren felt that Samantha was acting out her frustration in
going from one home to another.

All of Ms. Tingren's friends
spoke well of Mr. Gidley and were unaware of any serious conflict between him
and the defendant.  She had not told them of Samantha's disclosures regarding
conflict within her household.  None of her friends who testified were aware of
the circumstances of Mr. Gidley's prior marriage and none have seen the dark
side of him.

At trial, Ms. Tingren denied any
incidents of conflict or violence between herself and Mr. Gidley.  However, she
earlier admitted (at her examination for discovery in July 1992) that she did,
on numerous occasions, leave the house following conflict with Mr. Gidley.

Ms. Tingren described a good
relationship between Mr. Gidley and  Samantha.  They have engaged in many
activities together and she did not perceive that he favoured Dougie over
Samantha.  She said that after some visits with the plaintiff, Samantha had
bitten and kicked him and said "you're not my Daddy."

I have omitted reference to a
number of allegations against the plaintiff which appear to have been made for
the first time in Ms. Tingren's direct testimony.  I  placed no weight upon
them because they were not put to the plaintiff during his evidence and thus he
was given no opportunity to deny or explain them; they were not supported by
any independent evidence.

Ms. Tingren's credibility was
seriously shaken when she was called as an adverse witness in the plaintiff's
case. She admitted having a bank account with Vancouver City Savings which she
had failed to disclose in her statement of property sworn on April 8, 1992.
Although she denied having any other bank accounts, she subsequently conceded
that she had a small amount of money in an account at Bellis Fair in
Bellingham.  She refused to either agree to obtain the relevant banking
documents or to sign an authorization to enable Mr. Schuman to obtain the
documents in order to verify the amount in the account.   She denied the
suggestion that she had opened it to deposit money as part of a plan to make
arrangements in the United States in case she was unsuccessful in this
litigation and laughed incredulously (as did her counsel.)  A former friend,
Ms. Cividino, testified that Ms. Tingren had disclosed such a plan to her.  Ms.
Tingren testified that her mother had given her a small amount of money to open
an account to buy clothing for the children.  In her direct examination more
than a month later, she produced the bank statements which indicate an initial
deposit of $450.00 in January 1992 and a present balance of $358.14.

She denied that she had received
any money between 1990 and 1992 other than from Mr. Gidley, Mr. Gurvin, family
allowance and some brief part-time work.  She also denied that she had an
interest in any estate.  However,  Mr. Schuman produced documents which
established that she was one of the beneficiaries of the estate of her
grandmother who died in 1989.  On March 6, 1990, she signed a consent to
probate of the estate.  She testified that she did not receive the inheritance
but instead gave the whole amount to her brother.  She was unable to recall the
amount.

In November 1990, Mr. Gidley
purchased a home in Delta.  He and Ms. Tingren and the children lived there
until 1992 when he purchased a home in Richmond.  Ms. Tingren testified that
she had no interest in either property and that she had neither given money nor
loaned money to Mr. Gidley to buy the property.

When she was asked if her
brother, Scott Tingren, had loaned Mr. Gidley the money to buy the property,
the defendant initially declined to answer.  She subsequently conceded that Mr.
Tingren had loaned Mr. Gidley approximately $18,000 to purchase the Delta home
but she claimed to know no details of the loan arrangement.

At her examination for discovery
in July 1992, she had testified that Mr. Gidley bought the house in October
1990 solely with his own funds.  She said then that she and Mr. Gidley had no
set plans and that they were unsure if they would remain together.  At trial,
Ms. Tingren admitted that the latter statement was untrue and that they have
shared a firm intention to marry since at least July 1990.  The former
statement is clearly untrue.

Notwithstanding Ms. Cividino's
evidence to the contrary, Ms. Tingren denied having told anyone that she had
avoided taking an interest in the property in order to qualify for Legal Aid
representation for this case or to avoid any order for costs against her.

Her counsel declined to
cross-examine Ms. Tingren on those issues pursuant to Rule 40(20)
notwithstanding Mr. Schuman's advice that he would invite the Court to draw an
adverse inference from the defendant's failure to provide an explanation at
that time rather than at a later date at which time she would be presumed to
have discussed her evidence with counsel.

When she gave her direct evidence
six weeks later, she pointed out that she had waived her inheritance in favour
of her brother in March 1990 before this litigation was commenced in July.

Mr. Scott Tingren, who now
resides in the Lower Mainland,  testified that he supported his sister
financially for several years and, while he hoped to be repaid, he did not
really expect that to happen.  He received $40,000 from his grandmother's
estate: 1/2 of which was Ms. Tingren's portion.  After receiving her share
"for debts owed," he considered himself to be "fully and
completely repaid."

He was unable to recall any of
the details of the purported discussion of the debts or his insistence that
they be paid and I did not find his evidence convincing.  He said that he had
loaned her about $10,000 between 1983 and 1986; a further sum of approximately
$1,500 for two trips back east in 1988 and 1989; about $3,500 - $4,000 since
May 1990 and other "increments of money -- mainly cash."  During that
portion of his evidence, Mr. Tingren was evasive, repeated the questions, and
stalled before answering.

Mr. Tingren reluctantly conceded
that he had loaned $19,500 to Mr. Gidley but insisted that it was from his
portion of the estate and not from his sister's share.  He said that he had
offered Mr. Gidley the money on his own initiative as a personal loan to enable
him to purchase the Delta house.  He believed that his sister was not competent
to handle that sum of money and that Mr. Gidley would look after her and
Samantha.  They had no discussion as to the interest rates or the amount at
maturity or the date that the loan would be due; Mr. Scott obtained no promissory
note or other documentary evidence of the loan.

Mr. Tingren  volunteered the
statement that his sister was not aware of the financial arrangements between
himself and Mr. Gidley.  I do not accept his evidence.

Although Mr. Tingren initially
testified that he did not know whether or not his sister was on the title of
the home in Delta,  in cross-examination, he admitted that Ms. Tingren had told
him that the home was in Mr. Gidley's name alone.

Ms. Tsumura, a friend of Ms.
Tingren who is employed at Royal Trust, had referred Mr. Gidley to a loans
officer at that institution.  She testified that in order to buy a house, the
downpayment must be cash and not borrowed funds.  The downpayment could be
money acquired by a gift but not by any repayable loan.  She was never told of
any debts or loans involving Ms. Tingren's brother.

No satisfactory explanation was
given for the undocumented, interest-free loan from Scott Tingren to Jim
Gidley.  In my view, there is no explanation other than the obvious one that
Ms. Tingren wished to hide the fact of her interest in the property by
transferring her inheritance to Mr. Tingren which he in turn loaned to Mr.
Gidley to purchase their family home in Delta.  I assume that her motive for
wishing to hide that interest relates to this lawsuit -- either to enable her
to qualify for Legal Aid or to avoid an award of costs.

Ms. Tingren was also
cross-examined with respect to her relationship with Mr. Gidley.  She denied
that she had ever left the house and stayed overnight with friends because of
conflict between them.  She agreed that she had left the home on occasion for a
few hours to "cool down" after disagreements but she denied that she
had ever been threatened or frightened by him.  When pressed, she subsequently
conceded that she had left the home as a result of conflict with Mr. Gidley and
stayed overnight or for a weekend with friends or her brother.  She insisted
that the stress was the result of this litigation.  Samantha has witnessed
these arguments but Ms. Tingren insisted that they were verbal and not
physical.

Ms. Tingren testified that she
was aware of the "messy divorce" between Mr. Gidley and his ex-wife,
Ms. Carroll, but she believed his assurances that the allegations of mental and
physical abuse levied against him were unfounded.  She understood that he did
not refute the allegations so that he could obtain a faster, cheaper divorce.

THE PLAINTIFF AS A PARENT:

Mr. Gurvin is 47 years of age.
He is employed in the family jewellery store which is owned by his mother.  His
hours of work are flexible.  He testified that he now has the full support of a
large extended close family.  His mother has developed a very close
relationship with Samantha.

Ms. Grafton noted that during the
visits which she supervised, Samantha was always excited and happy to see her
father.  She considered the plaintiff to be a good parent:  he was patient with
her; she was responsive to his discipline; and they were comfortable and
affectionate with each other.

Ms. Scott described Mr. Gurvin
and Samantha as sharing "a wonderful relationship."  She spoke highly
of Mr. Gurvin's parenting skills.  She described Samantha as always eager to
come to visit her father and sad to leave.  Ms. Scott testified that the
plaintiff does not initiate negative comments about Ms. Tingren or Mr. Gidley.

I accept the evidence of the
plaintiff and the access supervisors that he and Samantha have a warm, loving,
positive relationship.  He is patient with her and she apparently adores him.
According to the supervisors and friends who have observed them together, Mr.
Gurvin disciplines Samantha calmly and effectively.

Rosalee Hardin, a cousin of the
plaintiff,  has been a family court counsellor and probation officer since
1974.  She has observed the plaintiff with Samantha on four occasions and
praised his parenting skills.  She considered them to have a warm,
affectionate, comfortable relationship.

Mr. Gurvin was shocked and
horrified at the allegations that he may have harmed Samantha in any way.  He
was concerned that Ms. Tingren had apparently discussed the ongoing court
proceedings with her.  After the contempt proceedings were commenced, she had
asked him "why are you going to put Mummy in jail?"

When Samantha made statements
which suggested that someone had prompted her to "recall" incidents
of sexual abuse or discussed this litigation with her, he tried to comfort her
and refrained from questioning her.

Samantha complained of a sore
vagina and bottom on three occasions during the period that Mr. Gurvin's access
was supervised.  As a result of his concern that something had happened to her
at home, his counsel sought and obtained an order on March 10, 1992 obliging
Ms. Tingren to report any further complaints of abuse to Dr. Elterman.

I accept his evidence that he was
deeply concerned for Samantha's safety and welfare.  He was distressed by the
statements she made which indicated that she was being mentally and physically
abused at home.

The plaintiff has had a number of
girl friends and casual encounters over the years but, with the exception of
one woman who often accompanied Mr. Gurvin and Samantha on access visits with
her son, those relationships have not affected Samantha.  His present
involvement with Nicole Forest has endured over a year and appears to be
serious.  She testified at trial and impressed me favourably as someone who
would have a positive influence upon both Mr. Gurvin and Samantha.  She is 32
years of age, intelligent, poised, and well-educated. I accept her evidence
that she and Samantha have a good relationship.  Ms. Forest sees Mr. Gurvin as
a caring and loving parent who is patient and involved.  She said that he does
not make negative comments about Ms. Tingren.

Mr. Gurvin testified that he
wished to take on full parenting responsibility for Samantha but agreed that
Ms. Tingren should have ample access.  He expressed a concern that access be
supervised at first because Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley have persistently
influenced Samantha negatively.

DR.ELTERMAN'S ASSESSMENT
:

After Ms. Watty's recommendation
that he be retained, Dr. Elterman  was engaged jointly by Mr. Katz (who acted
for Mr. Gurvin in the early stages of this lawsuit) and Ms. Andres-Auger in
October 1990.  At trial, he agreed that he had worked with Mr. Katz on other
cases but he rejected Ms. Andres-Auger's suggestion that he considered this
case as a referral primarily from Mr. Katz.

Ms. Tingren reported three
concerns to Dr. Elterman in November 1990: (1) her belief that the plaintiff
was saying negative things about her and Mr. Gidley; (2) her concern that the
plaintiff was drinking and driving; and (3) her apprehensions about sexual
abuse.  Those latter concerns centred on the bathing episodes and sleeping in
the same bed and a further comment by Samantha which suggested that the
plaintiff had put ointment on her reddened vagina.  She reported that Samantha
had begun masturbating 6 months earlier (which would be shortly after the March
overnight access visit) and had a reddened vagina as a result.  Ms. Tingren
described Samantha as "a mess" after the visits.

At a later date, she related the
incident in which Samantha had a red and swollen vagina and a circular ring about
5" in diameter around her anus.  She said that the child had difficulty
sleeping and that Samantha had told Mr. Gidley that the plaintiff had hurt her
vagina.  She described further examples of Samantha's aberrant behaviour.  Dr.
Elterman read the reports of the doctors who had examined the child.

In his interview with Dr.
Elterman, Mr. Gidley expressed his belief that Samantha had been sexually
abused either by the plaintiff or by someone else while she was with the
plaintiff.  He also described marks on her body and certain acts and statements
which had a sexual connotation.

Dr. Elterman described Samantha
as "a very outgoing, extremely intelligent child with a large vocabulary
and a strong desire to express herself."  He found her a remarkable and
delightful child to be with.  She displayed a keen sense of curiosity, and she
was observant and emotionally open.  However, he observed a marked difference
in her between his first interviews with her in November and December and the
later interviews in February.  By that time, she had become less happy,
spontaneous and verbally open.

Dr.
Elterman concluded that Samantha had very strong and positive feelings towards
her father and that she was confused by the conflict between her parents.
After interviewing Mr. Gurvin, Ms. Tingren and Mr. Gidley, and spending
several sessions with Samantha, he expressed the following opinion in his first
report of February 10, 1991:

I did not hear from
[Samantha] that she had been touched or hurt by Mr. Gurvin.  I also did not
observe any seductive behaviour, any sexual acting out or any physical
self-consciousness or reluctance on her part.  Moreover, I found in her a child
who is bright, extremely outgoing, and has a wonderful relationship with all
three adults in her life.  I believe that much of what has been brought forward
as evidence of sexual abuse has been the result of a systematic
misinterpretation of what the child has said and done.

He believed that certain sexual
behaviour which is normal to children had been misinterpreted.  He expressed
the opinion, in his first report, that it was improbable that Mr. Gurvin had
sexually abused his daughter.

Pursuant to a Court Order of
January 23, 1992 which was made over Ms. Tingren's strong objections, Dr.
Elterman prepared an updated report which was concluded on August 29, 1992.  He
remained of the opinion that sexual abuse was improbable.

As a result of his later
interviews with Samantha and Ms.

Scott, Dr. Elterman concluded that
there were  protection concerns regarding Mr. Gidley and Samantha.
Specifically, Samantha told him that Mr. Gidley hit her, called her a bad girl,
yelled at her,  locked her in her room when her mother was out, and fought with
her mother.  Ms. Scott told him that she had seen Samantha cower when Mr.
Gidley raised a hand to her.

Dr. Elterman testified that he
followed his set practice of taking a history from the main participants in
this type of custody and access dispute.  In his interview with Mr. Gidley, he
gained the impression (which Mr. Gidley clearly intended to convey) that Mr.
Gidley had been married on one previous occasion and that the marriage had broken
down "because the parties had lost interest in one another."  Dr.
Elterman agreed that if he had known that Mr. Gidley had brutally assaulted his
previous wife, that he had harassed and threatened her after the marriage, and
that he had threatened to commit suicide, those facts would have been relevant
to his assessment.  I find those facts were established on the evidence of Ms.
Carroll, the ex-wife of Mr. Gidley.   When Mr. Schuman outlined the development
of the relationship based upon Ms. Carroll's evidence, which I accept, Dr.
Elterman characterized it as the "battered wife syndrome" or the
typical pattern of an abusive relationship.  I conclude that those facts
substantiate Dr. Elterman's protection concerns which were based upon Samantha's
statements to him and Ann Scott's reports.

Ms. Tingren did not disclose to
Dr. Elterman any conflict or violence in the household.  She did not tell him
that she had left the home from time to time because of conflict with Mr.
Gidley.

DR. PENFOLD'S TREATMENT OF SAMANTHA:

In February 1992, Ms. Tingren
asked Dr. Penfold, an experienced child psychiatrist, to assess the possibility
of past sexual abuse.  Because Samantha was so young, and because the alleged
incidents had happened so long ago, she was unable to form any opinion.  She
then addressed the behaviour concerns expressed by Ms. Tingren (disobedience,
temper tantrums, screaming, demanding behaviour, fears, poor sleep patterns,
and aggressive behaviour towards Dougie) and she has been treating Samantha in
play therapy since that time.

Dr. Penfold attributed the
primary cause of Samantha's behavioural difficulties to being torn between two
parents.  She identified additional stresses: the birth of her brother, gaining
a step-father, and the move to a new home.  As she was unaware of any conflict
and aggression in Ms. Tingren's household, she did not consider the possibility
of those factors as a cause.  She considered the family unit to be experiencing
stress resulting from this litigation and from financial stresses caused by Ms.
Tingren's inability to work.  She was not given the opportunity to interview
the plaintiff.

I agree with Dr. Penfold's
strong recommendation that a mental health professional and both parents should
remain involved in Samantha's care on an ongoing basis.  She expects Samantha's
behavioural difficulties to subside if both parents make a positive
contribution to their daughter's well-being.  She fervently believes that
co-operation between the parties is essential to Samantha's best interests.

CONCLUSIONS:

(a)
The
defendant's allegations of sexual abuse by the plaintiff:

Throughout the trial, I was
extremely concerned that there may some validity to the defendant's concern
that Samantha could have been sexually abused by her father.  I do not consider
an allegation of sexual abuse to be the type of issue that could properly be
determined on "the balance of probabilities" in this case.  I have no
hesitation in saying that if the evidence raised a reasonable suspicion that
such abuse had taken place, or might take place, I would "err on the safe
side" by denying the plaintiff either custody or unsupervised access.

Mr. Gidley made a complaint of
sexual abuse to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on February 1, 1991.  The matter
was referred to Detective Pranzl who was then a member of the sexual offence
squad.  Detective Pranzl talked to Drs. Louie, McTaggart and Mitchell, and Ms.
Tingren and Mr. Gidley.  He attempted to interview the plaintiff who, on his
lawyer's advice, declined to speak with him.  He videotaped a 50-minute
interview with Samantha on February 15, 1991.  He presented his evidence to
Crown Counsel who advised him that no criminal charges would be laid.

The videotape was shown in
Court.  Samantha was just over three years old at the time of the interview.
Although she is clearly an articulate, intelligent little girl, she was
obviously reluctant to discuss the topics that Detective Pranzl wished to
address.  When asked if she knew what a "private part" was, whether
anything was bothering her, when she last saw her father, and what she did with
her father, she was silent, evasive, avoided the questions, climbed out of her
chair and under the table, and actually left the room.  If she answered any of
his questions, she generally said "yes".  Detective Pranzl agreed
that she was clearly uncomfortable with the subject matter.  When Detective
Pranzl asked her how she played doctor with Daddy Michael, she told him to get
his "doctor stuff".  That statement would be consistent with the
plaintiff's explanation to Dr. Elterman that they played doctor using the
stethoscope listening to each other's chest.  Detective Pranzl gave her a doll
and asked her to show him how to play doctor.  She said "check where the
bum is", and "undress" as she undressed the doll.  She put her
face within millimetres of the vaginal area of the doll and said "look in
your bum" and "look in the 'gina."   As she had been examined by
a number doctors in the preceding two weeks, I would expect those examinations
to determine her perception of how one "played doctor."

The video of Detective Pranzl's
interview with Samantha and his subsequent evidence, which included his opinion
that the investigation had never completed, raised concerns as to possible
sexual abuse.  As a result, I requested that Dr. Elterman view the video before
giving his testimony.  Dr. Elterman expressed the opinion that the interview
was done poorly by the police officer who asked leading questions and who
failed to establish a rapport with her.  He suggested that Samantha's evident
avoidance of Detective Pranzl and his questions could be explained by her
irritation with the number of interviews she had been subjected to or her
reluctance to answer the questions "yes" or "no" because of
the conflict between her mother and her father.

I conclude that the video does
not establish sexual abuse by the plaintiff.

Further concerns arose from the
fact that Samantha had been taken to the doctor because she had a red ring
around her anus.  At trial, Dr. Mitchell testified that he wrote down the
possibility of sexual abuse as a cause because of the mother's concern and not
because the child had said anything to suggest abuse.  Examinations a week
earlier and on April 22, 1991 were negative.  On December 3, 1991, Dr. Mitchell
observed Samantha to have a perio-anal rash.  He referred her to a
dermatologist but he has no record of any report from the specialist.  He
agreed that there were dermatological diseases which could cause erythema of
the anus.

In his testimony, Dr. Mitchell
agreed that it was possible that the red ring could have been caused by
penetration or attempted penetration, by a hot object, or by a suction device.
In response to a question by Ms. Andres-Auger, he stated that the diameter of
his stethoscope was 5-6 cm. in diameter.  On the basis of that evidence, the
defendant suggests that the red ring was caused by Mr. Gurvin using his
stethoscope while playing doctor.  I reject that suggestion.  Moreover, that
allegation was not put to Mr. Gurvin in cross-examination.

In cross-examination, Dr.
Mitchell agreed that fecal matter in a child's underpants could cause such a
rash.

A number of other doctors
examined Samantha as a result of Ms. Tingren's concerns of sexual abuse but
they were not called upon to testify at trial.  I conclude that the red ring
was not caused by any sexual abuse or impropriety by the plaintiff.

In considering Samantha's
complaints of a sore bottom and a sore vagina, it is necessary to keep in mind
the fact that she made those complaints on a number of occasions both before
and after her visits with the plaintiff which were supervised.

I do not purport to understand
the cause of Samantha's unusual and distressing habit of tying people up but I
do not find that it is related to any sexual impropriety by the plaintiff.

On the basis of all of the
evidence, I am satisfied that there are no grounds for the assertion that Mr.
Gurvin did, or is likely to, sexually assault Samantha.

I find that Ms. Tingren has
planted the suspicion of sexual abuse in Samantha's mind by attempting to
remind Samantha of incidents which did not in fact occur.

(b)

The defendant's persistent denial of
access:

Dr. Elterman expressed the view
that Ms. Tingren confuses her relationship with Mr. Gurvin and Samantha's
relationship with him.  I agree with that assessment.  Ms. Tingren's anger and
frustration have clouded her perception of Mr. Gurvin as a father and those
emotions have caused her to fight bitterly towards her goal of ridding both her
life and her child's life of him.  She sincerely believes that Mr. Gurvin has
forfeited his rights as a parent to Samantha.  In consequence, she has
thwarted, and attempted to destroy, the independent father-daughter
relationship which has developed since the end of her relationship with the
plaintiff.

That course of conduct failed to
recognize the fact that any "right to access" was Samantha's right to
see her father rather than the plaintiff's rights which Ms. Tingren
unilaterally decided that he had forfeited.

Ms. Tingren, probably as a result
of her personal anger and frustration with Mr. Gurvin, has done everything to
interfere and prevent him from having a relationship with his daughter.  As a
result of actually denying access unilaterally, Mr. Justice Warren found her to
be in contempt of Court following a lengthy hearing.
In
Tremblay

v.
Tremblay

(1987),
1987 CanLII 147 (AB QB)
,
10 R.F.L. (3d) 166 (Alta. Q.B.)
Mr. Justice
Trussler stated that serious questions are raised about the fitness of a parent
who refuses access.   In my view, a parent who discusses the adversarial
aspects of the litigation with a young child attracts further doubts as to his
or her fitness.

(c)

The plaintiff's protection concerns
regarding Samantha in her

present environment:

Mr. Gidley denied that he had
ever beaten Samantha although he did concede that he had spanked her, locked
her in her room on one occasion, told her that she was bad on occasion and had
lifted his hand to her -- although he had not struck her.  He emphatically
denied that he has ever hit Ms. Tingren and he stated that he did not believe
that Samantha had made such a disclosure.

While emphatically denying that
he has ever struck Ms. Tingren, he admitted that as a result of arguments or
conflict, she has left the house -- as has he.  He described very little
conflict in their house.

During his interview with Dr.
Elterman, he attributed the breakdown of his 10-year marriage to "a loss
of interest in each other over the years."   In fact, Mr. Gidley has been
married twice.  He was married in l971 at the age of 21 for 3 years and again
from 1979 until 1988.  His second wife, Ms. Carroll, petitioned for divorce on
grounds of physical and mental cruelty.  In the course of those proceedings,
she obtained a restraining order.  Even if the allegations of cruelty were
untrue,  Mr. Gidley deliberately misrepresented the circumstances of the
breakdown of his marriage to Dr. Elterman.  He also denied depression, suicide
attempts, problems with alcohol or drugs, and anxiety or a quick temper.  The
evidence suggests that he did experience those difficulties either during or
upon the breakdown of his marriage.

Mr. Gidley stated that because he
and Ms. Tingren were told that Dr. Elterman would be used against them, he was
not forthcoming with him.

During the trial, Mr. Schuman
became aware of those divorce proceedings.  Mr. Gidley testified at this trial
that he had intended to countersue Ms. Carroll on grounds of irreconcilable
differences but that he had not contested the allegations of cruelty after he
received legal advice that his choice was to go through a long court battle or
"not fight it."  That evidence was untrue.  He  filed an answer and
counterpetition in which he specifically denied all allegations of threats or
assaults and sought a divorce on grounds of the breakdown of the marriage.

In cross-examination, Mr. Gidley
denied that he had struck Ms. Carroll although he admitted that, in the course
of his pushing her away in self-defence when she attacked and provoked him,
"she would subsequently get hurt."  He said that he never
"intentionally" hit her.  He admitted that it was possible that he
ran after her when she fled from him into the bathroom and that he broke down
the door.  When asked if he had made threats to his wife since their separation
in 1987, he replied initially that he did not recall and then denied that
suggestion.

In light of those allegations and
denials, Mr. Schuman subpoenaed Ms. Carroll to testify as a rebuttal witness at
trial.  Ms. Carroll testified that he had phoned her on two occasions during
this trial to enquire if she had been asked to testify.  He told her not to say
anything if she was contacted.  Because she was upset and scared, she retained
Ms. Auerbach as counsel to apply to set aside the subpoena or to apply for
directions to protect the witness.  Mr. Gidley, who denied threatening Ms.
Carroll, admitted that he telephoned her on two recent occasions to ask her if
she had been contacted to testify in these proceedings.

Ms. Carroll described a good
relationship with Mr. Gidley in the early days which slowly degenerated into an
abusive relationship.  The violence escalated from verbal criticism to pushing
and shoving and finally to punching.  At first Ms. Carroll tried to stand up to
him but she became submissive because she was afraid that he would kill her.
She weighs about 100 pounds less than he does.   She testified that he had
harassed and threatened her after the separation and twice threatened suicide.
On one occasion he threatened to "blow her away."

Mr. Gidley  offered a number of
explanations for his ex-wife's allegations:  her medical problems which include
anorexia and an underactive thyroid, her inability to have a child during their
marriage, and the earlier birth of a son she gave up for adoption.  While those
difficulties have affected Ms. Carroll's life, they are unrelated to Mr.
Gidley's abusive behaviour.  I found Ms. Carroll to be a truthful witness.

Dr. Elterman believes that Samantha
has witnessed conflict between her mother and Mr. Gidley in the home.  Samantha
made similar comments both to Ann Scott and to Dr. Elterman with respect to
"stopping Jim from hitting Mummy."  Dr. Elterman  considered Ms.
Scott's observations to be honest, neutral observations which mirrored his
own.  I share his view that such conduct is intolerable and indefensible.  He
cited research which establishes that children who witness domestic violence
suffer the consequences of being the victims of violence in much the same way
as children who have themselves been beaten.

I conclude that the protection
concerns identified by Dr. Elterman are well-founded and that they jeopardize
Samantha's physical and psychological well-being.

I find that the conflict and
stress in the Tingren-Gidley household is an equal or greater source of
difficulty for Samantha than the stress and tension of the ongoing custody
battle.

CONCLUSIONS:

Dr. Elterman has had the unique
opportunity of interviewing and testing Samantha and the three adults in her
life.  On the basis of all of the evidence that I have heard, his description
of her as a "robust, wonderful child" rings true.

The Court's primary concern is,
without doubt, the best interests of Samantha.  I am persuaded that the
protection concerns identified by Dr. Elterman are real concerns.  That factor,
together with Ms. Tingren's continued refusal to permit a relationship between
Samantha and her father mitigate strongly against Ms. Tingren as the custodial
parent.  While Ms. Tingren has been Samantha's primary caretaker and is deeply
bonded to her, I believe that Samantha also has a close and loving relationship
with her father.  He is able to offer her a good home, involvement in an
extended family, and the peace and security of a stable home which she
presently lacks.

Although Dr. Elterman agreed with
Mr. Schuman that there would be some advantage to removing Samantha completely
from the conflictual environment of her mother's home, he cautioned that such a
benefit must be weighed against the overriding importance of maintaining her
relationship with both parents.  I accept his considered opinion that Samantha
requires continued contact with both of her parents and that she should not be
cut off from either of them.  Her greatest fear is to lose contact with one of
them because she loves and needs them both.  To lose either parent would be
emotionally devastating and extremely harmful.  She requires reassurance that
she can continue to see both parents on an ongoing basis.

DECISION:

On the basis of my conclusions
that the allegations of sexual abuse against Mr. Gurvin are groundless, that
Samantha is exposed to conflict in her present home which is harmful to her,
and that Ms. Tingren has tirelessly and continuously interfered with Mr.
Gurvin's access, I have concluded that the best interests of Samantha at the
present time will be met by transferring custodial status to her father.  I
find that he is a caring and concerned father who has developed, in the face of
significant adversity, a close and loving relationship with his daughter.
While Ms. Tingren has been Samantha's primary caretaker and they are deeply
bonded to one another, Samantha also has a close and loving relationship with
her father.  He is able to offer her a good home, involvement in an extended
family, and, most importantly, the peace and security of a stable home which
she presently lacks.

Mr. Gurvin will have custody of
Samantha.  Ms. Tingren will have access which, for the first three months, will
be supervised by the Greater Vancouver Mediation and Supervision Services or
such other person or persons as agreed by the parties or by order of this
Court.  Weekly reports are to be prepared and delivered to both parties or their
counsel within the following ten day period.  Copies of all reports are to be
produced to the Court in conjunction with any application dealing with access.
Ms. Tingren may exercise access during the three-month period from 9:00 a.m. to
5:00 p.m. every Saturday and from 3:00 p.m. to 7:30 p.m. on Wednesday evening.
She will bear the cost of those access arrangements.  The parties may agree to
alternative or additional times.  After three months, unless the parties
consent to additional access arrangements, I will review the access with a view
to granting unsupervised access and overnight access.

While I find that Samantha's
behavioural difficulties have resulted primarily from the conflict in her
mother's home, she has also been affected by the on-going court battle between
her parents.  The parties also have vastly different styles of parenting.  I
agree with Dr. Penfold that Samantha requires consistency in parenting.
Accordingly, it will be a term of the order that Samantha continue in therapy with
Dr. Penfold, or such other mental health professional as agreed by the parties
or approved by the Court.  Both parents are to involve themselves in Samantha's
treatment and co-operate in that process.  The costs of that therapy are to be
shared equally by the parties.

As a further term of the order,
both parties are restrained from removing Samantha from the jurisdiction of
this Court without the written consent of the parties or an order of this
Court.

The time has come for both
parties to recognize the fact that their paramount parental duty is to provide
Samantha with two secure, loving and stable parental relationships.  There must
be no implied or express threat that she will lose one of her parents.  Both
parties know full well that continued anger and hostility between them will
have a negative effect upon Samantha.  The courts have repeatedly recognized
the fact that a refusal to grant access (in the absence of proper cause) raises
serious questions about the fitness of that parent.  I believe that Mr. Gurvin
will facilitate reasonable and, when appropriate, generous access to Ms.
Tingren.  However, if either parent sabotages the other's parental relationship
with Samantha, it will be necessary to revisit the issues of custody and
access.  I recognize the fact that it will take some time and a lot of hard
work to overcome the elements of bitterness and acrimony that have surrounded
this fight for a number of years.  Ms. Tingren testified that there is a bond
between Samantha and Mr. Gidley but none between Samantha and her father.  I
conclude that a strong bond has developed between Samantha and the plaintiff
and it is time that Ms. Tingren recognized that fact.

I expect that the parties will
have to take guidance from Dr. Penfold, or another mental health care
professional, as to how they can devote their energies to Samantha's best
interest instead of continuing the battle.  Ultimately, the parties, and not
the Court, must govern the care and nurturing of Samantha.  Ideally, that process
will now begin.  If Mr. Gidley is to be a permanent part of Ms. Tingren's life,
then he should be part of that process.

Counsel have liberty to apply
with respect to any terms of my order regarding access.  I propose to remain
seized of this matter for a period of one year.  However, if I am unavailable,
applications may be brought before another Judge or a Master.

"M.J.
ALLAN, J."

Vancouver, British Columbia

December  23, 1992
